stories.title: Confidence expressed in minister amid O'Connor sacking
stories.summary: Minister for Education Hildegarde Naughton has said she has "absolute confidence" in Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, echoing the Taoiseach and Tánaiste in recent days as the fallout from Anne O'Connor's sacking continues. However, she stopped short of expressing confidence in the HSE board following its dismissal of Ms O'Connor. Taoiseach Micheál Martin has called for a fuller account of Ms O’Connor’s dismissal and has stopped short of expressing confidence in the board. Tánaiste Simon Harris this week also stopped short of expressing confidence in it and said it was essential that the board answer questions before an Oireachtas committee. She said the board would appear before an Oireachtas committee next week. Ms Carroll MacNeill said on Wednesday that she did have confidence in the board.

stories.title: Liam Kearney named EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026
stories.summary: Liam Kearney, the CEO and co-founder of engineering company The Revive Group, was named the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026 at the annual awards at Powerscourt Hotel in Enniskerry, Co Wicklow. Founded in Tipperary in 2020, The Revive Group's operations include manufacturing machinery for wastewater infrastructure, refurbishing existing trucks to extend their working life, patented recycling technology and data services that support the circular economy. Revive's factory is fully off-grid, complete with its own rainwater harvesting, wastewater treatment plant and power generation. The business is doubling in size every year and is now targeting €100m in turnover. It is active in around eight markets and is entering new territories every six to 12 months. The company directly employs around 100 people in Ireland. EY also presents a Special Recognition Award to recognise an exceptional contribution to communities and society across the island of Ireland. This year Andy Moran accepted the award on behalf of the Mayo football team and wider Mayo GAA community, recognising the determination, ambition and collective effort behind Mayo's first All-Ireland Senior Football Championship title in 75 years.

stories.title: Ireland must be ruthless to back up their Springboks win
stories.summary: There's been a trend with Ireland in the last year that big wins and big performances have been followed by a regression. Last year's record win against Australia came a week before a brutal defeat to South Africa, the record win away to England in February was followed by a stuttering performance against Wales, and after hammering Scotland to finish the Six Nations, they needed a miraculous comeback to beat the Wallabies in their Nations Championship opener. Even this month, Ireland started their run of November games with a slick win at home to Argentina, before going through the motions a week later against Fiji. That might go some way to explaining Andy Farrell's team selection for this evening's renewal with Australia, which rounds off their Nations Championship campaign. After such an attritional game against the Springboks last week, and with a six-day turnaround to what is essentially a fifth-place play-off against the Wallabies, there was an expectation that the Ireland head coach would use the final game of 2026 as an opportunity to get some gametime into the wider squad and wrap some of the frontliners in cotton wool. Instead, Farrell has run his selection back, with just two changes made from the XV that started last week's win, both changes enforced through injury to Mack Hansen and suspension for Dan Sheehan.
stories.rssSummary: Given last week's result, the bar has now been set for this Ireland team, and with such a strong side picked to go again this weekend, a similarly strong performance is the expectation – rather than hope – at Allianz Stadium, writes Neil Treacy

stories.summary: Laureate for Irish Fiction Éilís Ní Dhuibhne delves into contemporary Irish fiction on a journey of exploration to highlight literature emanating from every county in Ireland. In Island of Imagination, she speaks to some of our best contemporary literary fiction writers about their novels and short stories and their writing lives and ponders the question 'What makes a good story?'. In this episode, Éilis talks to novelist Sarah Gilmartin about her acclaimed novels Dinner Party and Service and her writing practice - watch below: This event was recorded in association with Limerick Literary Festival. stories.title: DWTS welcomes back pro dancer and introduces a new face
stories.summary: For the 10th season, fans will see "a mix of returning favourites, a brand-new face, and a much-anticipated comeback" in the pro dancer line-up. "Fan-favourite Salome Chachua will make her eagerly awaited return to the series after taking last season off to welcome her first child," said DWTS. "The Georgian dancer has previously reached the final on three occasions, partnering rugby star Jordan Conroy in 2022, Wild Youth singer David Whelan in 2024, and Mrs Brown's Boys actor Danny O'Carroll in 2025. "Joining the Irish ballroom for the first time is Italian dancer Domenico Romagnolo. "Having started dancing at the age of 12, Domenico went on to establish an international competitive career in ballroom and Latin dancing. "His competition highlights include reaching the semi-finals of the Under-21 Rome Dance Cup, finishing in the top 40 at the Universal Championships and claiming runner-up at the 2021 Amateur Shining Star Cup.

stories.title: Back to Ibiza at 49: Older, wiser and still dancing
stories.summary: Returning to Ibiza's clubs after 18 years, Deirdre Mullins discovers that good music, room to dance and the right company still make a great night out. When Leftfield drops "Open Up", I look at my friends. Everyone is smiling. For a moment, it feels like I’m back in my Capel Street flat during my student days, same music, same friends. But we’re actually in Ibiza, and it’s dusk at the outdoor club 528. Above the sail-like canopy, the sky glows red and orange. A warm breeze moves through the crowd. People dance on the steps around the dance floor. There’s space to move, not a phone in sight, and it’s not even 8pm. We’re here to celebrate two 50th birthdays. It’s been 18 years since I last went clubbing in Ibiza, and I was here with this same group back then. We exchange looks that say it all. Coming back to Ibiza was a great idea. I remember clubbing in Ibiza in the noughties as being full of freedom and excitement: dancing with friends, meeting people from all over the world, and never knowing where the night would lead. Before this trip, my Instagram feed was full of videos of crowded dance floors and people filming the DJ on their phones. It made me wonder if I’d still enjoy the nightlife. stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he has asked Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, in a fresh shift in tone towards the Russian leader he called his friend just last week. Mr Trump said he had made the request to Mr Putin when they met in China last week, adding that he thought it would help lead to a deal to end Moscow's grinding war in Ukraine. Mr Trump's comments come a day after he hosted NATO chief Mark Rutte in Florida, after which the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war. "During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," Mr Trump said on his Truth Social network. Mr Trump said he had done so "in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly." The statement did not specify which territories Mr Trump meant - and did not specifically include Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022, kicking off the largest war in Europe since World War II.

stories.title: AirBaltic offers crew exit, demotion or secondment
stories.summary: Latvia's airBaltic is offering staff a choice between leaving, accepting demotion or a secondment to a Papua New Guinea airline, according to emails seen by Reuters and two people with knowledge of the process, as the carrier cuts costs during Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. The airline has been hit hard by soaring jet fuel prices in the wake of the US-Israeli war with Iran after it started the year without the hedging agreements in place that would have insulated it from those rising costs. It entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in September and said in October it planned to cut 500 to 700 jobs. Peer Norse Atlantic yesterday said its finances were critical, sending its shares down 80%. AirBaltic, which is majority-owned by the Latvian government, began contacting some cabin crew in October, offering them a choice between termination and a demotion, the emails showed. It offered other employees incentives to leave voluntarily. Pilots were presented with similar options as airBaltic, which once aimed to expand its fleet to 100 jets by 2030, now plans to reduce its 54 Airbus A220-300s to 36 by the end of this year, according to the emails and the two people. Some were told to choose between a secondment to Papua New Guinea's Air Niugini and termination, the emails showed. One of the people added that others were asked to give up their line training captain status, which carries additional pay.

stories.title: English in no rush to make call on what comes next
stories.summary: Mark English has said he's in no rush to decide on whether or not he will try to carry his incredible 2026 form into the LA Olympics picture in two years' time. It brought English his sixth Euro individual medal – indoor and outdoor – but it was his first time standing atop the podium after he ran pretty much a perfect race. Naturally, when thinking of the 2028 Games, English's name will come up in dispatches, but he will be 35 when they roll around and the athlete said he's in no hurry to make any major commitments. "I know we've always thought in Olympic cycles in this sport, but even the Europeans this year, you know, with the Irish interest in it, it's been phenomenal to witness it," English said. "It's not just for me, but for Rhasidat (Adeleke), for Kate and for the rest of the team. But yeah, it's just about enjoying these moments. I heard recently how sometimes we don't enjoy these moments enough. "So it's just really about soaking it in and giving back to those people who helped me get to the point where I got to this year and really appreciating it.

stories.title: BBC announces tribute shows for Duran Duran's Andy Taylor
stories.summary: The BBC has announced tribute programming in honour of Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death. On Wednesday night the band announced Taylor had died aged 65. In a statement, the band said: "Andy Taylor, beloved husband, father and grandfather, has died following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer." Taylor helped shoot the award-winning New Romantic rock band, famous for tracks such as Hungry Like The Wolf and Rio, to superstardom in the 1980s. The BBC said it will be paying tribute to the musician with radio and TV programmes, including Duran Duran at the BBC on BBC Four at 9.30pm on Friday, 27th of November. The broadcaster said the show would be "a celebration of the finest performances and appearances by the New Romantic sensations on the BBC".

stories.title: Calls for regulation of tech-facilitated sexual violence
stories.summary: There will be calls for stronger regulation of tech companies to address technology-facilitated sexual violence at an event organised as part of Ireland's EU Presidency this morning. The conference, which will be hosted by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) and Ruhama, will examine the threats posed by rapid technological change in sexual violence and sexual exploitation. There is concern that online platforms, digital devices and emerging technologies, including AI, are increasingly being used to recruit, groom, exploit, threaten and control women and girls. Ruhama and the DRCC have called for greater enforcement of existing legislation and further regulatory action to ensure that technology companies are held accountable for making the digital world safe for women and girls. The 'Call to Action' by both organisations has been endorsed by the European Women's Lobby and members of Ireland’s Observatory on Violence Against Women. As part of an enhanced regulatory framework, it proposes that technology companies embed safety and users' rights protections into the design, development and operation of digital products, services and algorithms from the outset.

stories.title: Whatever happened to the working week?
stories.summary: Analysis: Take some time out from your day job to discover exactly how the working week come about - and where it might be going This is no longer your daddy or mammy's working week. A century on from Henry Ford giving his employees Saturdays and Sundays off, the working week and the workplace have changed beyond all comprehension. In the last few years, we have seen the emergence of such trends as hybrid working, the gig economy, the on-demand retail sector, quiet redundancies, micro-retirement, coffee-badging and quiet holidays. And all of this before we even mention the fact that AI is eyeing up your job..... This week, we're all set to tease out how the working week came about and where it might well be going. Taking time out from their day jobs to join presenter Edel Coffey to talk about all of our jobs and working habits are Dr Sabrina Fitzsimons (School of Policy and Practice at the Institute of Education at DCU), Dr Coleman Dennehy (Lecturer in Medieval & Early Modern History at Dundalk Institute of Technology) and Dr Laura Bambrick (Social Policy Officer for the Irish Congress of Trade Unions).

stories.title: Superb 65 sees McKibbin soar into second in Australia
stories.summary: A seven-under par 65 saw Tom McKibbin shoot up the standings at the Australian PGA Championship leaderboard into second place, though a bogey at the last is likely to see Liam Nolan miss the cut. McKibbin opened with 69 at the Lakes Golf Club in Sydney, but on Friday he shot himself into contention with a blemish-free round that included seven birdies. The 23-year-old signalled his intent at the first, picking up a shot on the par-four hole, with back-to-back birdies at the fifth and sixth. McKibbin, who has one previous win on the DP Tour, the 2023 Porsche European Open, really found his groove on the back nine. A birdie at the 11th started a run of three in four holes, while he signed off at the 18th with his seventh birdie to card a 65 and 10-under par overall. He sits three strokes off halfway leader, Nicolai Von Dellingshausen. The German shot an eight-under 64 to put daylight between himself and the rest of the field.

stories.title: Meet the Irish entrepreneur selling gelato in winter
stories.summary: It's said that a good salesman could sell water to a fish, but a greater challenge may be selling frozen treats on the Wild Atlantic Way in the depths of winter. Thankfully, it seems Ronan Galvin is up for the task. Handcrafted in small batches in Athenry and served at The Creamery in Salthill, Wild Churn is an artisanal brand bringing authentic Italian gelato to the Emerald Isle. "Wild Churn was created as something from the West, bringing a bit of hominess," he says, noting that the logo incorporates the waves that decorate our coastline. The business has been many years in the making, with Galvin coming from a storied background cheffing and producing in the UK and US before returning to Ireland, where he set up shop in a Galway café for the past 24 years. Although he was doing well selling commercial ice cream, he says the opportunity to create his own product was one he couldn't miss. "My passion is in making food," he explains. "I've been travelling back and forth to Italy and seeing what's out there. I have a great affinity for the Italians, and they love to see it being developed in Ireland. They have such passion for it."

stories.title: Macron accuses Le Pen of 'arrogance' in EU budget clash
stories.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has hit out against far-right leader Marine Le Pen, accusing her of "arrogance" for criticising attempts to finalise the EU's next budget before France's elections next year. EU leaders are locked in summit talks in Brussels to try to strike a December deal on the bloc's 2028-2034 budget, to avoid tense negotiations spilling into a year of elections across Europe - most crucially in France. Mr Macron himself raised the stakes by threatening to walk away if there is no deal before 2027 - prompting Ms Le Pen to hit back. "Our country is on the brink of default and social upheaval. Our leaders should be focusing on setting things right, rather than resorting to underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people," Ms Le Pen, frontrunner to win the upcoming presidential vote, wrote on X. Hours later, on the sidelines of the summit, Mr Macron said of Ms Le Pen: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected." It is not the first time the two have clashed over the budget.

stories.title: Hayes happy to realise camogie rather than Olympic dreams
stories.summary: In a different world, Laura Hayes could have the Los Angeles Olympics on her mind rather than the challenge of retaining the All-Ireland title with Cork, and attempting to propel St Catherine's to county success. To anyone who has chased the 26-year-old dynamo up and down the field over the years, it will come as no surprise that running was a real passion of hers. Hayes emerged from secondary school with two athletics scholarships to US colleges on the table in front of her. It was the ultimate sliding doors moment. Fast forward to last Saturday night and the former PwC GPA Player of the Year was nominated for the award that went to Cork team-mate Sorcha McCartan. Hayes ends the year with a third All-Ireland medal and fourth All-Star. For most of her time with Cork, her endurance and lightning speed was deployed from half-back, neutralising top-flight forwards by making them turn around as she split the posts or set up scores at the other end.

stories.title: Two companies behind McGregor stout record €2.43m losses
stories.summary: Two companies behind Conor McGregor's Forged Stout brand recorded combined losses of €2.43m last year. New abridged accounts filed by McGregor’s Forged Stout Production Ltd show that it recorded post tax losses of €2.2m last year Separate accounts filed by McGregor’s Forged Stout Distribution Ltd show that it sustained post tax losses of €166,662 for 2025. The combined losses at the companies last year are down sharply on the combined €7.7m loss for 2024 and the combined losses of €8.25m for 2023. Combined accumulated losses at the two Forged Stout firms at the end of 2025 totalled €18.38m as accumulated losses at Forged Stout Distribution totalled €10.3m while accumulated losses at Forged Stout Production amounted to €8.04m. A spokesman for Forged Irish Stout said: "We are very encouraged by the continued commercial progress of Forged Irish Stout, with growth of over 100pc in 2026 to date and expansion into 14 new markets."

stories.title: Moore: 'Inconsistent' Wallabies can still contend at RWC
stories.summary: Former Australia captain Stephen Moore believes time is still on the Wallabies' side to be contenders for the Rugby World Cup on home soil next year. Less than a year out from the tournament, the two-time world champions have struggled for any real consistency, with Les Kiss' side currently seventh in the world rankings ahead of this evening's Nations Championship finale against Ireland at Twickenham. The Wallabies almost beat Ireland in Sydney earlier this year, as Andy Farrell's side came from behind to snatch a dramatic 33-31 win in July, and they followed that up with a heavy defeat to France and a win against Italy, before Kiss took over the job from outgoing boss Joe Schmidt. Their 10 games since have continued to underwhelm; a win against South Africa capped off a decent start to life under the former Ireland assistant, while there were also two wins against Japan, and a draw and a win against Argentina, before their form plummeted. Heavy defeats to New Zealand in October were followed by losses against England and Wales in their northern hemisphere leg of the Nations Championship, but they ended that four-game losing run with a 29-26 win against Wales last Saturday, setting up a rematch with Ireland this week to decide fifth and sixth place in the tournament. "It's been like that for a number of years actually, you could say eight or 10 years it's been pretty inconsistent.

stories.title: Man due in court over robbery of cash-in-transit van
stories.summary: A man in his 50s is due in court today in connection with a cash-in-transit robbery that occurred in Dublin on Wednesday. A man wielding a suspected firearm approached the driver of a cash-in-transit van outside a premises in Crumlin, Dublin 12, at around 12.55pm on Wednesday. A sum of cash was reported as taken and the man fled the scene on an e-bike. After a follow up search on the same day, gardaí arrested a man in his 50s. He has since been charged and is due to appear before the Criminal Courts of Justice today. Gardaí said investigations are ongoing and are appealing to anyone who was travelling in the Crumlin area on Wednesday, between 12:30pm and 1.30pm, to contact them.

stories.summary: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon will seek the support of the ⁠centrist Opportunity Party to keep his ruling centre-right coalition in power after official results showed he fell just short of a parliamentary majority in this month's election. If Mr Luxon and his coalition partners cannot overcome policy differences with Opportunity, including on the environment and government investment, and any negotiations between other parties fail to produce a majority government, New Zealand would have to hold a fresh election. Political watchers said that while a return to the polls was unlikely, the negotiations to secure either a coalition or confidence-and-supply deal would be complex and could run into next year. "New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term," Mr Luxon told a news conference. "Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls." Opportunity's platform includes policies that cut against parts of the conservative coalition's agenda, including wanting stronger climate ‌commitments, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, tighter competition rules and ⁠a more interventionist approach to public investment.

stories.summary: Tadhg Beirne admits improving Ireland are still "nowhere near" being World Cup contenders. Ireland will bid to end a positive autumn campaign with four wins from four by beating Australia in Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off. Munster skipper Beirne, who will captain his country against the Wallabies at Twickenham, believes Ireland are making progress but wants to send a message to rival nations. "This campaign has very much been built on 'can we improve and get better quickly?' and I think we've been doing that, certainly," he said.

stories.summary: An Australian woman who used deadly fungi to murder relatives has asked Australia's top court to hear an appeal of her conviction and life sentence. Erin Patterson, aged 52, was last year found guilty of murdering her husband's parents and aunt in 2023, deliberately lacing their beef Wellington lunch with lethal death cap mushrooms. Last month, the Court of Appeal in the Supreme Court of Victoria rejected Patterson's attempt to quash her conviction. The High Court is her last opportunity to appeal her conviction. Patterson has consistently maintained her innocence, saying the deaths were an accident. Patterson's application to the High Court rests on some of the same ‌grounds as her Supreme ⁠Court action, according to court documents. "The Court of Appeal erred in its application of principles that justice must not only be done, but be seen to be done," said Patterson's appeal bid, filed by her lawyers on Friday.

stories.title: Europa League: Duran rides to Celtic's rescue in Portugal
stories.summary: Camilo Duran came to Celtic's rescue in Europe again after coming off the bench to head a late winner against Torreense in Portugal. The Colombian striker peeled off to the back post to meet a cross from fellow substitute James Forrest and send a downward header into the net in the 85th minute. Duran's 15th goal of the season earned a 2-1 victory over the Portuguese second-tier side and put Celtic on six points in the Europa League after his double off the bench inspired a comeback win over Besiktas last time out. Celtic took the lead in the ninth minute when Javi Vazquez sliced Jota's cross into his own net with Yang Hyun-jun right behind him. But the Portuguese Cup winners levelled 10 minutes later after some sloppy defending. Both Kieran Tierney and Colby Donovan had chances to deal with bouncing balls after Alex Alfaro hit the bar from 22 yards but they could not clear and Haiti international Dany Jean volleyed home. Celtic dominated second-half possession but clear chances were at a premium until Duran struck.

stories.title: Nvidia CEO Huang not a security threat - Trump
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump said that he had seen sufficient information that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a security threat. Mr Trump described his administration's intervention to save the scandal-plagued CEO's job as "a great thing" for the world. "I think he's absolutely fine," he told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate. Asked how he could be sure after the US Justice Department would not confirm whether it had conducted a thorough investigation into the CEO, Mr Trump said his belief was based on "information I have, which is a lot of information." Mr Huang, a key figure in the AI revolution, was forced to resign earlier this month after revelations that he had an affair with a business executive who reportedly has ties to Chinese intelligence and whose company may have helped China obtain advanced chips in violation of US export controls. His sudden resignation saw the stock price of Nvidia plummet, before a shock decision by the board to reinstate him saw a partial rebound.

stories.title: Ireland v Australia: All you need to know
stories.summary: When Andy Farrell ran over the perfect November in his head before Ireland's four Tests, the picture couldn't have been much sweeter than it has been so far. True, Ireland are playing for fifth or sixth when they face Australia at what is set to be a half-full Twickenham tomorrow night in the inaugural Nations Championship Finals series, but whatever happens in London, suddenly Irish rugby has the twinkle in its eyes again. Argentina and Fiji were always expected to be two victories, but winning margins of 30 points and 28 points set them up for a grandstand finale against South Africa last Saturday, even if it took a while for the side to click against Fiji. Last weekend, Aviva Stadium rocked, Rassie Erasmus punched tables in a Dublin hotel and Ireland looked deep into their souls and found the answers to withstand the World Cup champions. There is, of course, the possibility of a sour conclusion if Australia upset the odds tomorrow, but Farrell's side look well placed and should be brimming with energy and confidence. When all is said and done on Friday, it will be 70 days to the Six Nations and 311 days to the World Cup and after the last couple of weeks, those build-ups have become that bit more exciting.

stories.title: Fatal attack on man in care home 'unforgivable' - mother
stories.summary: A residential care company has admitted liability and failings in its care over the death of a 31-year-old man who suffered a catastrophic brain injury when he was assaulted in his own home by another resident. Paul Burke was a young man with Angelman syndrome and an intellectual disability, and he was assaulted on 26 February 2024 in Blanchardstown in Dublin where Mr Burke was living. The court heard that the rare genetic condition he had affected his nervous system and that he was non-verbal. He needed assistance in all activities including mobility. Avista Company Ltd had looked after these needs in residential care around the clock and there had been a staffing ratio of one staff member for each resident. However, on 26 February 2024, there was just one staff member in place who had not received induction training. After Mr Burke suffered a serious injury to the side of his head, it was several hours before this was recognised and an ambulance was called.

stories.title: Man who cares for wife with brain injury wins carer award
stories.summary: A Donegal man who has cared for his wife since she suffered a brain haemorrhage 35 years ago has been named as the Lidl Family Carer of the Year 2026. Hugh Brendan McDyer, from Glenties in Co Donegal, was just 38 when his wife Rose McDyer had a brain haemorrhage followed by strokes in 1991. Ms McDyer was left unable to walk or talk and Mr McDyer became her full-time carer while raising their young family. Their children were aged 10, four and three at the time. The awards ceremony held at College Green Hotel in Dublin today heard how Mr McDyer left his job to be able to provide round-the-clock care to his wife. He was also determined that his children would not miss out on their childhood, from football training to friendships, because of what had happened. His children had nominated him for the award with one of his daughters saying "these may sound like ordinary things, but doing them every single day, for 35 years, is anything but ordinary, he has never let her down".

stories.title: High Court refuses to sanction BAWAG acquisition of PTSB
stories.summary: The High Court has refused to sanction BAWAG's proposed €1.62 billion acquisition of PTSB because the lender failed to hold a separate meeting for minority shareholders to vote on the deal. PTSB shareholders, including the Government, which holds a 57.5% stake in the bank, approved the sale to Austrian lender BAWAG at a meeting in July. However, the High Court ruled that the remaining shareholders were entitled to vote separately on the scheme. The bank, the board of which recommended the offer in April, said it was considering the judgment and would make a further announcement in due course. BAWAG Group also said it is considering the judgment in a statement. Irish corporate finance company Axis Capital said on October 2 that it was considering making a rival offer of €3.20 per share, a 7.7% premium to BAWAG's offer, but that it had not secured financing for a possible approach.
